voiceover: Where did everything come from? Either the universe has always existed — or it had a beginning: a first moment before which there was, literally, nothing physical at all. The Kalam cosmological argument is just three lines. One: whatever begins to exist has a cause. Two: the universe began to exist. Therefore, the universe has a cause. Notice what it does not say — not 'everything has a cause,' only things that begin to exist. That precision is built in. Out of nothing, nothing comes. If things could pop into being from nothing, why don't we see it everywhere? Did the past stretch back forever, or begin? Two independent lines converge. Philosophy: you can't cross an actual infinite by adding one moment at a time. Picture Hilbert's Hotel — infinitely full, yet always room for one more. Science: the Big Bang traces the universe to a finite past. And in 2003, the Borde-Guth-Vilenkin theorem showed that essentially any expanding universe must have a past boundary. So the universe has a cause — one that brought all of space, time, and matter into being. It must be spaceless, timeless, immaterial, unimaginably powerful, and itself uncaused. And most plausibly, a mind that freely chose to bring it into being. The heavens still declare something.
